summary: Explains how to use packet delay variation metrics, which appear in many standards. The metric in RFC 3393 is very flexible, so this document guides which formulation to pick for particular uses and discusses how results should be interpreted.

eli5.summary: Packets sometimes arrive at uneven gaps, like a bus that comes early then late. This note helps people choose the right way to measure that unevenness and make sense of the numbers.

subtitle: Guidance on measuring and interpreting packet jitter in networks.

tldr.problem: Packet delay variation, or jitter, is measured in many standards, but the metric definition in RFC 3393 has considerable flexibility. Two main formulations (IPDV and PDV) are used, but their properties and applicability differ.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5481 compares Inter-Packet Delay Variation (IPDV), which measures change between consecutive packets, and Packet Delay Variation (PDV), which measures variation from the minimum delay. The RFC examines circumstances and uses for each form.
tldr.outcome: PDV is recommended for most applications like de-jitter buffer sizing and service-level monitoring. IPDV suits scenarios with clock skew or path instability. Choosing the right metric improves accuracy of network performance analysis.

today: RFC 5481 remains an informational guidance document for network operators and measurement practitioners. It has not been obsoleted and is actively referenced in network management and performance monitoring deployments.

sections.title: What is Packet Delay Variation
sections.content:
Packet delay variation is a metric that quantifies a network path's ability to transfer packets with consistent delay. The phenomenon is sometimes called jitter, though delay variation is more precise. All delay variation metrics are derived metrics: they compare the one-way delay of two packets to assess how their arrival times differ.

The RFC focuses on two formulations that have become widely used in active measurements. In Inter-Packet Delay Variation (IPDV), the reference is the previous packet in the sending sequence. In Packet Delay Variation (PDV), a single reference point is chosen, typically the packet with minimum delay in the sample. Both are compliant with RFC 3393, which allows multiple formulations through different packet selection functions.
sections.eli5: If you send packets down a network path, they should arrive at even intervals, like a metronome. IPDV looks at how much the spacing between each pair changes. PDV measures how far each packet's delay is from the fastest packet.

sections.title: Understanding IPDV and PDV
sections.content:
For a stream of packets numbered 1, 2, 3, ..., IPDV(i) = D(i) - D(i-1), where D(i) is the one-way delay of packet i. This formulation measures changes in inter-packet spacing. IPDV values can be positive, negative, or zero. The mean IPDV is usually zero unless a long-term delay trend is present.

PDV(i) = D(i) - D(min), where D(min) is the minimum delay observed in the sample. PDV values are always zero or positive, ranging from zero (for the fastest packet) to the range of the delay distribution. PDV essentially normalizes the one-way-delay distribution to the minimum delay.

These formulations have different sensitivity profiles. IPDV distinguishes short-term variations (on the order of inter-packet spacing) from longer-term variations. PDV does not distinguish these time scales within a single sample but provides a direct measure of the variation in queuing delay.
sections.eli5: IPDV is like looking at how much the speed changes between each pair of consecutive buses. PDV is like measuring how far behind each bus is from the fastest bus that day. They answer different questions about how uneven the service is.

sections.title: When to Use Each Form
sections.content:
For determining de-jitter buffer size, PDV is preferred. The range of PDV values (max - min, or the 99.9th percentile) directly indicates the buffer size needed. A de-jitter buffer aligns packets with the minimum delay to spend the maximum time in the buffer, which is exactly what PDV measures from.

For inferring queue occupation, PDV anchored at the minimum delay gives a distribution equivalent to the queuing time distribution. When the sample minimum coincides with the true path minimum, PDV reveals the variation in queue time.

For spatial composition (combining measurements from multiple path segments), PDV has a clear advantage. All validated composition methods use PDV; there is no validated method for composing IPDV.

For service-level agreements, the one-sided PDV distribution is superior. A constraint such as no more than x% of packets shall have PDV ≥ y ms is straightforward to specify and implement.

IPDV advantages appear in challenging circumstances. When appreciable clock skew is present between measurement points, IPDV has lower demands on clock synchronization accuracy because it compares delays over short intervals. IPDV may also help identify path changes when accompanied by packet loss, though it cannot detect loss-induced path changes.
sections.eli5: Use PDV to design waiting rooms (buffers) and to compare network quality over time. Use IPDV when your clocks are slightly off or when you want to track moment-to-moment speed changes.

sections.title: Measurement Stream Characteristics
sections.content:
Both IPDV and PDV can be measured using Poisson sampling (random arrival times) or periodic sampling (fixed inter-packet intervals). Periodic streams are often preferred because they reflect the traffic patterns of real applications sensitive to delay variation, such as VoIP with 20 ms spacing.

Periodic sampling allows simplifying assumptions and can approximate IPDV or PDV using single-point measurements at the receiver. The choice of inter-packet spacing influences whether short-range or long-range dependencies are observed and how the IPDV distribution shape is affected.

For storage-constrained measurement devices, the choice of which metric to compute in advance matters. Devices with limited memory may store only summary statistics rather than individual singletons. To support later PDV calculation, minimum and several largest delays should be retained.

Measurement interval length affects the results. For de-jitter buffer sizing and queue analysis, the measurement interval should align with the duration of user sessions of interest. Shorter intervals (minutes rather than hours) reduce effects of clock skew and path changes.
sections.eli5: Regular packet streams (like VoIP) work well for these measurements. Keep track of the fastest and slowest packets if your device has limited memory. Measure for periods that match how long users actually use the network.

sections.title: Handling Packet Loss and Path Changes
sections.content:
Packet loss affects the two forms differently. If every other packet is lost, IPDV produces undefined results for all pairs, while PDV produces valid values for all arriving packets. In general, PDV is less affected by packet-loss ratios and patterns.

When path changes occur (routing changes due to link failure or maintenance), lossless path changes typically affect only one IPDV value. PDV shows a bi-modal distribution; one mode represents each path. To isolate each mode, treat path changes as separate measurement intervals and use TTL or hop-limit changes to detect them.

When path changes coincide with packet loss, IPDV may show no change if no packet pairs span the event. PDV still produces results for arriving packets and reveals the bi-modal distribution. Having loss and delay measurements together helps determine which mode corresponds to which path.

For load balancing using equal-cost multiple paths (ECMP), PDV identifies multiple modes in the distribution more easily. If each mode can be associated with a specific path, PDV supports optimization decisions like steering VoIP traffic to the path with better delay variation.
sections.eli5: When some packets vanish, PDV still works but IPDV might get stuck. When the network switches to a different route, PDV shows two separate groups of results. Use this to figure out which groups belong to which route.

sections.title: Summary Recommendations
sections.content:
RFC 5481 provides a decision framework summarized in a comparison table covering multiple dimensions: challenging circumstances, spatial composition, de-jitter buffer size, queue estimation, and SLA specification simplicity.

PDV is recommended for: de-jitter buffer design, inferring queue occupancy, spatial composition, service-level agreements, heavy packet loss, load-balanced paths, and most general-purpose measurements.

IPDV is recommended for: scenarios with clock skew between measurement points, identifying short-term vs. long-term variations, and situations where path changes must be detected even under loss (though IPDV also has limitations here).

The choice depends on the measurement goal, the network conditions, and the available resources. For most modern applications, PDV is the better choice because it directly relates to de-jitter buffer sizing, supports spatial composition, and lends itself to simple SLA specifications.
sections.eli5: In most cases, use PDV. It's simpler, handles missing packets better, and directly helps you size waiting buffers. Use IPDV only if your clocks are not well synchronized or if you really need to track moment-to-moment changes.
